Perhaps a small use case, but nasm is used in UMD's compilers course ( [course]).

And while that in itself is maybe not particularly exciting, I think the underlying point is more that assemblers like nasm allow for the implementation of toolchains like this, where you have some assembly with some C code. While not common, I'm sure cases like this are also not exceedingly rare.

mentions.author: sankha93
mentions.story: Ask HN: What interesting problems are you working on?
mentions.text:
This is exactly how Compilers are taught at the University of Maryland. The class CMSC430 ( [course]) actually starts off with a Scheme (limited subset of Racket) and gradually grows the language to include more features. The first class compiles just numbers to x86 code, followed by arithmetic operations for numbers, building up to higher level features like function calls, pattern matching, and so on. See the notes at: [course]

This style of building compilers is called the Nanopass style ( [link]), making it much easier to teach.

Source: I was a TA for the earlier iteration of the class.
